The white-edged lyretail, Variola albimarginata, is a grouper species that attains a relatively large maximum body size among the Serranidae. For adult females, the ultimate standard length has been recorded at 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], a dimension that places this species among the mid-sized coral reef predators within its genus. The length at which females typically achieve puberty, measured as fork length, is estimated at 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters], based on allometric relationships derived from the closely related white grouper, Epinephelus aeneus. This size threshold marks the transition from a predominantly somatic growth phase to one that includes reproductive investment, though the onset of gonadal activity may vary with local resource availability. The neonatal wet weight, calculated from an egg diameter of approximately 0.95 millimeters, is remarkably small at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], reflecting the minute size of the pelagic eggs that are typical of epinephelid spawners.

The maximum recorded body mass for adult females of this species is approximately 4962 grams [Wwi = approximately 4962 grams], corresponding to the asymptotic wet weight derived from the length-weight relationship common to many serranids. At the onset of puberty, when females have reached a fork length of 30 centimeters, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is about 462 grams [Wwp = about 462 grams]. This considerable gain in mass between birth and maturity underscores the rapid growth trajectory that characterizes the early life stages of this reef-associated predator. Under stable thermal conditions typical of tropical reef environments, individuals require a substantial period to accumulate the somatic tissue necessary for successful reproduction. The relatively high ultimate body mass compared to other species in the genus suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes the attainment of a large body size before significant reproductive output commences, a pattern that is consistent with the known ecology of long-lived serranids.

This value is calculated from the total annual fecundity of a large female white grouper, adjusted for the ultimate body mass of the white-edged lyretail, and then divided across the number of days in a spawning season. The thermal regime of 27.7 °C reflects the typical sea surface temperatures of the Indo-Pacific coral reef habitats where this species is found, and small deviations from this temperature are likely to influence both the rate of oocyte development and the timing of spawning events. The relatively high daily fecundity suggests that females invest considerable energetic resources into gamete production once they have attained a large body size.

The complete life span of the white-edged lyretail, measured under natural thermal conditions of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], is estimated at approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days], or a full decade of life. This longevity is consistent with the slow growth and late maturation characteristic of many epinephelid species, which typically exhibit extended lifespans as a bet-hedging strategy in variable reef environments. The sustained water temperature is crucial for maintaining the metabolic rates that support such a long life, as cooler waters would likely reduce growth efficiency and extend the time required to reach sexual maturity. The combination of a decade-long maximum lifespan, late maturation at a fork length of 30 centimeters, and the production of thousands of eggs daily during the spawning season reflects a life-history strategy that balances high fecundity with extended somatic persistence. This pattern is typical of tropical reef fishes that face high juvenile mortality but enjoy relatively low adult predation rates once they achieve a large body size.

The ecological role of the white-edged lyretail as a piscivorous mesopredator is intimately linked to its life-history parameters. The large ultimate wet weight of 4962 grams [Wwi = 4962 grams] enables adult females to prey upon a wide size range of reef fishes and crustaceans, positioning them as important regulators of prey community structure. The estimated maximum daily reproductive rate of 2137 eggs per day [Ri = 2137 eggs per day] at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] thus compensates for the extremely high early mortality typical of a pelagic larval stage.
